title: Growing Places: Mobilising private finance for local nature recovery

content.content: Nature is fundamental to our lives and our economy. Healthy soils help us grow food. Rivers and wetlands provide clean water and help protect communities from flooding. And thriving habitats support wildlife and make the places where we live more resilient.
But nature is under pressure. After a summer of extreme heat, the need to restore nature and make our farms, businesses and communities more resilient is clearer than ever.

Restoring it at the scale we need will take all of us: government, businesses, investors, farmers, land managers and local communities. Public investment remains essential, but private finance also has an important role to play in supporting nature recovery.

I’m Will Lockhart, Deputy Director for Nature Markets and Investment at Defra. Earlier this year, I wrote about how we are building trust in markets that help investors channel funding into nature’s recovery.

Today, to mark Finance Day at COP17 of the Convention on Biological Diversity, we are taking another step forward with the publication of Growing Places: Mobilising Private Finance for Local Nature Recovery. This document sets out how we are working to help connect private finance with the needs and opportunities of places all across England and the UK.
Growing Places establishes the government’s overarching place-based approach to mobilising private finance for nature recovery and sustainable growth.

It builds on what we heard from our Call for Evidence on Expanding the Role of the Private Sector in Nature Recovery and the Voluntary Carbon and Nature Markets Consultation: businesses and investors need long-term certainty, the right incentives, and support to unlock investment in nature. Growing Places takes forward that work, focusing particularly on how we can make investment happen on the ground.

"The UK's ability to withstand climate-related risks depends on multiplying private investment in nature. This important document has the right recipe, and Government must take action to implement these plans with regulation to make sure polluters and businesses pay to restore the ecosystems that should defend us all against drought, flood, fire and crop failure". Richard Benwell, Chief Executive at Wildlife and Countryside Link.
From national ambition to local action
The idea behind Growing Places is simple: the people who know a place best should have an important role in shaping its future.

Local leaders, farmers, land managers, businesses and communities understand their landscapes and local economies. By combining that knowledge with a clear national framework and private investment, we can support healthier, more resilient places.

Growing Places, therefore, focuses on three areas: growing demand for investment in nature and resilience; building confidence in nature markets; and developing a stronger pipeline of local projects ready for investment.
Backing farmers and healthy soils
Farmers and land managers are central to delivering nature recovery. Healthy soils underpin food production as well as providing wider benefits for nature.

Through Soilshot, an initiative described in more detail in Growing Places to find and scale new ways to improve soil health, we will explore how private finance can support productive, resilient and sustainable farming. This follows a recommendation from Baroness Batters’ Farming Profitability Review.
Growing Places also describes how the recently announced private finance taskforce will also work with industry to increase private investment in sustainable farming in England.

This responds to calls from agri-food sector stakeholders, who highlighted the importance of clear policy, targets, and standards, blended finance and better environmental data to drive investment and environmental performance.
Investing in resilience
We also want to harness investment in nature to help make communities more resilient to flooding and other environmental pressures.

Growing Places sets out how we are working closely with the FloodAction Coalition to learn from its pathfinder projects in Cambridgeshire and Greater Manchester, including how nature-based approaches to flooding, water resources and water quality can be scaled into wider regional investment.

We can already see the potential of this approach in Yorkshire, where the Aire Resilience Company brings businesses, landowners and public bodies together to fund natural flood management. Public funding supports the upfront work, while local businesses contribute towards ongoing maintenance, including payments to land managers.

To complement this work, Defra will continue to support the Green Finance Institute to bring businesses and land managers together to explore how nature-based solutions can strengthen local economies. This will build on the Institute’s analysis of business demand and its more detailed work in Norfolk and Suffolk.

“Private finance can help restore nature at scale when we create sustained demand, credible long-term revenue streams and practical place-based delivery. Resilience has the potential to become an important part of that revenue base.” Rhian-Mari Thomas, Chief Executive Officer, Green Finance Institute.
Making it easier to invest in nature

Nature does not fit neatly into boxes. Restoring a wetland, for example, can create habitat for wildlife while helping to manage water and tackle climate change. But financing the project can be complicated when different funding sources want to fund different outcomes.

That is why we are publishing proposed principles in Growing Places for combining environmental payments. The aim is to make it easier to finance projects delivering multiple environmental benefits with multiple different payment streams, while maintaining transparency and environmental quality.

These are proposals, not changes to existing schemes. We want to hear from farmers, land managers, businesses, investors and others, so we will be holding webinars and roundtable discussions over the autumn and winter to help shape our approach to these principles. If you wish to share any feedback, or to take part in any relevant session, please contact us.
Growing a pipeline of local projects

Finally, investment needs a clear pipeline of projects to invest in. Growing Places outlines how we are working with Local Nature Recovery Strategy (LNRS) lead authorities to invest in delivery partnerships and project pipelines. We are also looking at further ways we might be able to support projects in becoming market ready.
The aim is to help more places turn their ambitions for nature into credible opportunities for investment, while ensuring those projects remain rooted in local environmental priorities.

As highlighted in Growing Places, this approach is already taking shape in the West Midlands, where a new Nature Investment Hub is helping package local nature projects and connect them with investors, turning the priorities in the region’s LNRS into action.
Earlier this year, I described our work to build England’s nature markets as a milestone, not a finish line. Growing Places is the next part of that journey.

At COP17 in Armenia, countries are focused on turning global ambition for biodiversity into delivery. At home, we are doing the same: bringing together local knowledge, public investment and private finance to restore nature and build more resilient places for the future.

title: Looking at the bigger picture: how to make your woodland work in the landscape

content.content: England has such a great diversity of landscapes. From the mountains, hills and lakes of the Lake District to the patchwork of heathland and woods in the downs.

Landscape has played a significant role in shaping our national identity. In fact, the 18th-century English Landscape Movement and its leading designer, Capability Brown, are recognised worldwide for their naturalistic style and informal designs.
In this blog, I'll share the importance of landscape and woodland design principles to ensure your woodland design complements its local surroundings with guidance from the UK Forestry Standard.
Why landscape matters
Landscape is not just about how a place looks but how it reflects the relationship between natural features, human activity and how people experience an area.

An understanding of landscape context and how to apply good design practice is fundamental to creating a quality woodland that meets your objectives and society’s needs, while complementing and enhancing our diverse landscape character.
The UKFS states that:
Integrated woodland design: a holistic approach

Integrated design brings together specialisms often considered separately, in a coordinated way. It is particularly beneficial for woodland creation, that involves such a wide range of specialists from foresters, land agents and landscape architects to ecologists, historic environment specialists, the public and statutory stakeholders.
Whatever the objectives and scale of your woodland – integrated design has 3 key elements you should follow:
Understand the landscape context

Landscape context describes the characteristics of the wider landscape including the physical landform, existing vegetation, land-use and heritage of an area. It helps us to understand the setting of a site and how it relates to its surroundings.
National Character Area profiles produced by Natural England are a good starting point for understanding landscape context, and the strategic environmental objectives for a landscape.
Landscape is not just limited to our protected landscapes (national parks and national landscapes), it applies everywhere.

Local authorities often produce their own landscape character assessments. Some local authorities, community forests and protected landscapes have developed specific plans for woodland creation that identify opportunities and sensitivities through woodland strategies or local nature recovery strategies. For example, the Great Northumberland Forest's landscape research project considers opportunities for a tree-rich landscape.
Apply the 7 UKFS design principles
The 7 UKFS design principles help ensure that new woodland enhances landscape character and will often support wider objectives such as biodiversity and long‑term resilience.

These principles provide a lens for making decisions. Whether you are designing a community woodland, a habitat restoration project or a productive forest, they help to ensure that your new woodland fits the surrounding landscape. The principles include:
1. Spirit of place

This identifies what makes a location distinctive, in terms of its geology, landform, cultural history, vegetation patterns and visual qualities so woodland can reinforce the site’s inherent character rather than overwhelm it.
2. Unity
Ensures new woodland integrates visually and ecologically with its surroundings. Unity helps connect habitats and strengthen patterns across the landscape.
3. Landform
Landform influences woodland shape and the balance between open ground and canopy. Slopes will also dictate drainage and therefore tree species choice.
4. Pattern of enclosure
Recognises historic and ecological significance of field boundaries, hedgerows, walls and woodland edges. Designs should reinforce or sensitively adapt existing enclosure patterns.
5. Scale
Considers how woodland fits within the broader landscape – from expansive uplands to intimate valleys, and how internal spaces evolve as the woodland matures.
6. Shape

Organic, landform‑led shapes can help woodland sit comfortably within the landscape, particularly in open uplands but lowland agricultural landscapes may be informed by a more dominant pattern of enclosure with woodland in more formal shelterbelts.
7. Diversity
Promotes both visual and ecological variety. Diversity supports resilience and habitat richness, while remaining sensitive to priority habitats.
Follow a woodland design process

When designing a new woodland, a landscape character appraisal can highlight the qualities that make a place distinctive. By integrating ecological mapping and historic environment data, this ensures that biodiversity and landscape considerations sit side-by-side.

In sensitive landscapes such as protected landscapes (national parks and national landscapes), historic estates, designated sites or major catchments – landscape character appraisals are important for demonstrating that new woodland creation will protect these important features in the landscape.

Important features and zones within the site that are less suitable for woodland planting are identified, appraised and mapped. Features such as non-woodland priority habitats, trees and scrub, historic monuments and the wider-historic or cultural context or popular viewpoints. Opportunities can then be explored to create connectivity between these elements and to retain links outside the site. A knowledge of underlying soils is also critical for trees to thrive.
Consultation
Plans and drawings are important tools when you engage with stakeholders and the local community, to be able to explain the option(s) developed through the design process.

A site will not be seen in plan form: supporting materials such as 3D perspectives and panoramas can help visually communicate your woodland design. Supporting materials do not need to be complicated – simple, annotated photographs can convey most of your thoughts and may aid your thinking.
Designing your woodland
When designing your woodland, it’s important to consider:
Zoning

Zoning is a useful technique that can be used to support woodland concept development by matching woodland objectives to site conditions. For example, productive woodland stands are best located on richer, more sheltered soils, while fragile or species-rich habitats are often associated with thinner soils. Conversely, open, visually prominent or historically significant areas may be less suitable for woodland creation.
Open space

Species choice and planting arrangements are the most obvious decisions to make on site, but a good alternative starting point could be to consider the evolving network of open space within your woodland. A productive woodland should incorporate open space and a strong framework of broadleaf trees to create wildlife corridors that connect with the wider landscape.

Such a strong network of open space could fulfil many long-term objectives such as, site access, recreation or linking non-woodland habitat. You need to consider fencing and other tree protection in your design to mitigate and manage mammal damage to your trees.
Woodland edge

Planting does not necessarily need to go right to the boundary, as woodland edges are really important from a landscape and ecological point of view. For example, you can shape woodland edges to deliver high levels of light for invertebrates and ground flora. You can use rides and glades to create movement corridors for butterflies and birds. Also, planting a varied structure helps trees to be more resilient to high winds, drought and diseases.
Your woodland: a legacy for the future
Woodlands enrich our landscapes in many ways alongside the range of benefits they provide to wildlife, society, the economy and the natural environment.

Designing woodland is a creative process with problem solving at its heart. There are challenges to overcome to achieve establishment, whether they are through our changing climate or the threats from pests and diseases. However, when you plant a woodland that compliments the landscape, you will create a lasting legacy for future generations to enjoy.

description: Robin Gray, Landscape and Woodland Design Advisor, explains how designing a woodland with landscape in mind and following the UK Forestry Standard, can result in greater efficiencies and benefits for you and the environment.
